content: The ounce, abbreviated as oz, originates from the old Italian word onza, now spelled oncia. It is a unit of mass used in various systems, including the imperial and United States customary systems. The size of an ounce can vary depending on the system in which it is used. The two most commonly used ounces today are the international avoirdupois ounce and the international troy ounce. International Avoirdupois Ounce The avoirdupois ounce is the most widely used ounce in modern times. It is defined as one-sixteenth of an avoirdupois pound, which is equivalent to 437.5 grains. In 1958, the United States and the Commonwealth of Nations agreed to standardize the international avoirdupois pound as exactly 0.45359237 kilograms. Consequently, the international avoirdupois ounce is precisely 28.349523 grams. This unit is commonly used in the United States for measuring mass. International Troy Ounce The troy ounce, abbreviated as t oz, is defined as 480 grains. This makes the international troy ounce exactly 31.1034768 grams. Historically, there were 12 troy ounces in a troy pound, which is now obsolete. For gold, specific terms are used: A fine ounce refers to a troy ounce of gold that is 99.5% pure (also expressed as 995). A standard ounce refers to a troy ounce of 22-carat gold, which is 91.66% pure. This consists of 11 fine ounces of gold and one ounce of alloy material. Apothecaries' Ounce The apothecaries' ounce, now obsolete, was equivalent to the troy ounce. It was historically used by apothecaries, who are now referred to as pharmacists or chemists. Maria Theresa Ounce The Maria Theresa ounce was introduced in Ethiopia and some European countries. It was equivalent to the weight of one Maria Theresa thaler, which is 28.0668 grams. This weight also defined the value of one Birr, a currency still in use in Ethiopia and formerly in Eritrea. Metric Ounces In some countries, the ounce has been redefined to align with the metric system. For example, in the Netherlands, the ounce (referred to as ons in Dutch) has been standardized as 100 grams. Similarly, the avoirdupois pound (pond in Dutch) was redefined as 500 grams. These metric definitions were adopted with the introduction of the metric system and are still informally used, particularly in cooking and grocery contexts. Indonesia has inherited and adopted the Dutch metric values, with 1 ons equaling 100 grams. This is formally recognized in the Indonesian national dictionary and taught in elementary schools. In East Asia, there is a traditional unit of mass called the tael, which is also referred to as an ounce. Its value varies, but in China, it has been standardized to 50 grams.
